summary: Round 1's F1 is three-quarters closed and measurably so: I re-ran its exact mutation (LocalSequencer open(prevEpoch, 0)) plus seal(epoch+1), seal(prevEpoch-1) and drop-the-seal, and the checker now reports link and/or I2 for all four, killing aTakeoversTWOChains... and aCleanRunViolatesNothing. F2, F3, F4, F6 and F7 are closed (F7 verified by deleting the I1 arm: the new fixture dies). The author's headline number reproduces exactly -- ROUGH(0.05,0.05,0.1), 80 rounds, 3 pods: seeds 45 and 79 of 0..79 violate, 4 violations, all I2, 362ms for 80 seeds. BUT the fourth door is still open, and it is F1's door one token over. The fix answers 'was my predecessor sealed FOR me' from the predecessor, and still answers 'did I have a predecessor at all' from the successor's own word, via two early returns that emit nothing. MEASURED: log.open(0, 0) -- every chain denying it has a predecessor, every stream restarting at 0 at all 18 failovers -- leaves checkChain EMPTY for all 240 chains across all 80 clean seeds, and aCleanRunViolatesNothing green. Same for dropping log.open entirely. That is verbatim F1's failure scenario, and crossEpochOffsetsChecked() == true (asserted at InvariantsTest:159 as the API's honest-reporting claim) still over-states what a clean report means. Also measured, and the reason 2/80 is quiet: ROUGH runs barely run -- 0 to 21 commits and 1 to 5 takeovers against the clean run's 76 and 18, seed 17 committing ZERO and reporting clean -- and the anti-vacuity assertions are on the CLEAN run only. No production file is touched, so no object-store request rate changes; the harness's own check phase is O(pods*rounds) LISTs on MemoryBinStore, measured at 4.5ms/seed, i.e. ~4.5s for M4.13's 1,000 seeds inside its 60s budget.

findings.line: 170-177 (the two early returns in inheritedOffsets); flag at 67; consumed at 81; asserted at InvariantsTest.java:159-168
findings.finding: The revision closed 'was my predecessor sealed FOR me' (checkLink reads the predecessor's own SEAL: continuedAt, prevSeq, and the seal's existence -- all three verified dying under mutation) but left 'did I have a predecessor at all' answered entirely on the successor's word. Two early returns emit no violation: line 170 returns when entries.getFirst() is not a Continue, and line 173 returns when opening.prevEpoch() < 1. Both then seed nextOffset with an EMPTY map, so every delta in that chain is checked against 0 and a first delta at offset 0 is accepted. The protocol facts that would refuse this are already relied on ELSEWHERE IN THIS FILE and not restated as predicates: the comment at 192-195 walks back 'by the arithmetic the protocol guarantees: epochs advance by exactly one per acquisition', and Continue's javadoc says every chain above epoch 0 has a predecessor and that a first leader writes prevEpoch=0. So for epoch > 1 a CONTINUE naming epoch 0 is a protocol violation, and a chain carrying a CommitDelta with no CONTINUE at slot 0 is a chain that was never opened -- neither is checked. The line-173 comment ('A truthful "there was no predecessor"') is true only at epoch 1; the code applies it at every epoch.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED on the staged tree, compiling the mutants into a separate output directory so the tree was never touched. (a) LocalSequencer.java:110 log.open(prevEpoch, prevSeq) -> log.open(0, 0): every chain claims no predecessor, so every stream restarts at 0 at every failover -- I2, NFR-11 and acceptance criterion 4 broken at all 18 takeovers of seed 7. Result: checkChain returned EMPTY for every chain, aCleanRunViolatesNothing PASSED, and a sweep of CLEAN seeds 0..79 (240 chains) reported 0 violating seeds. The only assertions that died were InvariantsTest:147 (resumed.firstOffset() expected 6, was 0 -- a PRODUCTION-side assertion, not the checker) and an incidental zombieWrites count. (b) Deleting log.open outright: identical -- checker silent, clean sweep 0/80. This is round 1's F1 failure scenario verbatim, reached by a one-token variant of the very mutation F1 named, and it is the same consequence: M4.13's 1,000-seed sweep, whose entire evidence is violations().isEmpty(), would run green over a system that reassigns every offset at every failover, while crossEpochOffsetsChecked() reports that the join WAS examined. Both mutants do die in 5-13 pre-existing LocalSequencer/CommitLog tests, so the SYSTEM is guarded; what is unguarded is the checker's claim, which is exactly the standard round 1 applied to F1. Fix, and I verified it cannot false-positive: over 5,840 chains from 160 runs (CLEAN and ROUGH, seeds 0..79) every CONTINUE names exactly epoch-1 and no chain ever carries a CommitDelta without a CONTINUE, so (i) for epoch > 1, report link unless opening.prevEpoch() == epoch - 1, and (ii) report link when a chain holds any CommitDelta but does not open with a Continue -- which leaves the burned epoch (a lone Seal at slot 0, 1,327 of those 5,840 chains) correctly silent.

findings.finding: The F1 fix added four new predicates/mechanisms and a fixture for only two of them. MEASURED as surviving mutations of the staged tree (Invariants.java mutated in a scratch copy of the test source set, InvariantsTest + CommitProtocolSimulationTest run against it): (1) the new 'gap' arm at 124-128 -- disabling it leaves everything green; nothing builds a chain whose delta resumes ABOVE the high-water mark, so the half of the I2/gap split that was newly introduced is unfalsified (aHOLEInTheChainIsReported covers the SEQUENCE gap, kind 'chain', not the offset gap). (2) the continuedAt-mismatch arm at 257-260 -- disabling it leaves everything green; the two link fixtures cover 'no SEAL' and 'wrong prevSeq' but not 'the SEAL names a different epoch'. (3) the never-opened walk-back at 196-199 -- disabling it leaves everything green, and this is the mechanism that produces the ONLY violations the sweep reports: with it disabled the checker inherits nothing across a burned epoch, agrees with production, and seeds 45 and 79 go quiet. (4) the upTo fold at 204-218, which the javadoc at 210-213 names as the independence mechanism ('FOLDED TO THE PREDECESSOR'S OWN SEAL ... not to the successor's claim') -- removing the break leaves everything green. For contrast the arms that ARE pinned each died: I1, chain, I5, I2-rewind, no-SEAL link, prevSeq link, and transitive inheritance (deleting the recursion at 214 fails aCleanRunViolatesNothing).
findings.failure_scenario: This is round 1's F7 one commit later: M4.13 runs 1,000 seeds and reports 'I1-I5 hold', and four of the clauses that report are branches no test can distinguish from absent. The concrete loss is (3): a future reader trimming the walk-back as dead weight -- it looks like a loop over chains that carry no information -- silences the only class of violation the harness currently finds, and the sweep goes from 2 violating seeds to 0 with nothing failing. The named regression tests M4.13 is supposed to leave behind for seeds 45 and 79 would then pass for the wrong reason.

findings.finding: F5's fix buys the toggle-independence it was asked for -- each class draws unconditionally from its own stream, so disabling one no longer moves another's fault positions -- but the three seeds are three CONSECUTIVE integers (3s+1, 3s+2, 3s+3) fed to java.util.Random, whose scrambler makes nearby seeds produce phase-locked LCG streams. MEASURED over 100,000 seeds at p=0.05, comparing the unreachable and ambiguousPut streams draw index by draw index: at draw 1 each fires ~4,830 times and BOTH fire 4,778 times where independence predicts ~250 (a 19x excess -- if one fires, the other almost certainly does); at draws 2, 3, 20 and 50 both fire 0 or 1 times where independence predicts ~250 (mutual exclusion); draw 10 is back to 3,667. So the classes are not independent coins at any draw index, they are alternately locked and exclusive. Separately, seed*3+k collides across the sweep: the simulation's own Random(seed) is bit-for-bit the unreachable stream of another seed (verified: Random(4) equals the unreachable stream of seed 1), which holds for 2,999 of the seeds in 0..2999, and the first-draw correlation between the simulation's stream and the store's is 0.46.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13's criterion 1 wants per-class evidence and a 1,000-seed sweep that explores fault COMBINATIONS. Under this seeding, combinations at a given call position are systematically over- or under-represented by more than an order of magnitude: the ambiguous PUT landing while the store is also unreachable -- the interleaving the class javadoc at 17-23 says the file exists for -- occurs at draw indices where the streams happen to be locked and is IMPOSSIBLE at the indices where they are exclusive. A sweep tuned to the declared probabilities will therefore report a fault mix it never ran, and the failure is invisible because every run is still deterministic and replayable. One line fixes it: derive the three seeds with a mixer rather than by adding 1, 2, 3 -- new SplittableRandom(seed).split() three times, or splitmix64(seed, k) -- which also removes the cross-seed stream collision.

findings.line: 120-131 (the clock-advance comment and its cited measurement); CommitProtocolSimulationTest.java:25-41 and 63-97
findings.finding: The comment at 120-128 says time must pass when nobody leads or the simulation DEADLOCKS, and cites as the broken case 'a faulted run made 6 commits and 3 takeovers where the clean run made 85 and 18'. MEASURED on the staged tree with the fix in place, ROUGH(0.05,0.05,0.1) at 80 rounds and 3 pods: seeds 0..19 make 0 to 21 commits and 1 to 5 takeovers, reach epoch 47-71 with 47-67 chains of which a third are burned, and seed 17 makes ZERO commits with 1 takeover and reports no violations. Those numbers are indistinguishable from the ones the comment offers as evidence of the bug, so the citation cannot tell a reader fixed from broken: the deadlock is gone, the vacuity is not. The reason is structural and worth writing down -- start() issues a LIST plus a GET per entry per ANCESTOR chain (the transitive crossing M4.9 owns), so P(start survives a 5% per-call unreachable) collapses as history grows and each round burns an epoch instead of committing. Meanwhile the anti-vacuity assertions are attached to the CLEAN run (aRunACTUALLYCommitsAndFailsOver..., commits > 10 and takeovers > 2, on CLEAN), and the ROUGH test asserts only that faults fired and zombieAttempts is positive -- it asserts nothing about progress. The backlog row does disclose that the two faulted-run progress assertions fail today and are deferred to M4.16, so this is the missing NUMBER rather than a hidden gap.
findings.failure_scenario: It is the answer to 'is 2 violating seeds of 80 plausible or suspiciously quiet'. I reproduced the count exactly -- seeds 45 and 79, 4 violations, all I2 -- but it is quiet because almost nothing happens: a run that commits 2 to 8 times cannot often reach the burned-epoch-after-a-committed-chain shape that produces the I2. When M4.16 fixes the protocol and M4.13 sweeps 1,000 seeds, 'I1-I5 hold across 1,000 seeds' will be a statement about clusters that committed a handful of segments each, and the row will read as far stronger evidence than it is. Recording the measured commits/takeovers per faulted seed in the row (or gating the ROUGH tests on the same progress floor the CLEAN one has, once M4.16 makes it reachable) is what keeps the claim honest.

findings.finding: Round 1's F8 -- two tests taking java.time.Clock.systemUTC() in the commit that introduces SimulatedClock -- is NOT closed: aChainAREALSequencerProducedHasNoViolations at :57-60 and the start() helper at :150-155 both still pass Clock.systemUTC() into LeaseConfig. It is inert today (nothing in either test depends on expiry, and a stall long enough to lapse the 10s TTL still permits the takeover these tests need), which is why it is minor and not more.
findings.failure_scenario: The next test added to this class that DOES depend on expiry -- and M4.16/M4.17 are both about expiry -- will copy the helper at :150, get a wall clock, and become the kind of failure the SimulatedClock javadoc says this module refuses to have: a seed that is a story about a flake rather than a permanent regression. Passing the SimulatedClock the commit already ships costs one argument and removes the wall clock from the class entirely.
